summary: This unit teaches you to work well with the people around you in a villa or small property: the guests you serve and the colleagues you work beside. You will learn to greet and listen to guests, speak and use body language clearly, answer the telephone, find out and meet guest needs (including guests who need extra help), handle complaints and difficult guests, work in a team, hand over between shifts, solve conflict, and take instructions and feedback from your supervisor.

blocks.p: A guest may forget the colour of the bedspread, but will remember how the people at the villa made them feel. Your skill with people matters as much as your skill with a mop, a tray or a cooker. This unit is for HOSPITALITY VILLA/PROPERTIES SERVICES LEVEL 2 trainees, and it supports every other unit you will do, because every task in a villa involves a guest, a colleague or both.

Ask for feedback and learn from it

Use clear, simple English and cope with language differences
Handle the telephone and messages
Answer professionally, take accurate messages
Pass messages on in writing
Find out and meet guest needs
Ask open questions and listen
Help families, older guests, guests with disabilities, and guests with dietary needs
Treat all cultures with equal respect
Handle complaints and difficult situations
Listen, apologise, act and follow up
Stay calm with rude guests and know when to call your supervisor
Respond safely if a guest is hurt
Work well in a team
Share work fairly, help others, join briefings

Listen and ask
Act on the need
Check the guest is happy

blocks.note: How you are assessed: theory papers (multiple-choice questions, short answers and essays) and group role plays in the Centre's training villa: a guest arrival, a special request and a complaint, then a team briefing, a duty plan and a shift handover. The assessor watches your words, your body language, your listening and your teamwork.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.note: Use made-up guest names in role plays and written records. Do not use real people's names or details.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: **Customer service** is meeting, and where possible going beyond, what the guest needs and expects. At a villa the guest is often a family or small group who share your space for several days. They notice small things. A good villa feels like a welcoming home that is well run.

ul: **Meeting expectations**: a clean room, a hot shower, a meal at the time promised.
**Exceeding expectations**: giving better service than the guest expected, such as a cold drink waiting on arrival or a note with the day's weather.
**Failing expectations**: late, careless, or not caring. This is what gets into reviews.

blocks.note: Good service does not mean agreeing to anything. If a guest asks for something unsafe or against the rules, you say so politely and offer a safe alternative. It also does not mean serving the guest who tips best first.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.h: Small actions that show you care

ul: Smile, look at the guest and use a warm greeting that fits the time of day.
Learn and use the guest's **name**. It makes the guest feel recognised and valued.

Notice and pass on special occasions. If a guest mentions an anniversary or birthday, tell your supervisor so a small surprise can be arranged. Do not tell all the other guests or ask what the holiday cost.
Do small things before you are asked: refill the water jug, offer an umbrella when rain starts.
Say 'Certainly' and do the job **promptly**. Saying yes and then doing it at the end of your shift is not good service.

blocks.p: A **service standard** is a written promise about how a task is done, for example 'answer the phone within three rings' or 'greet every guest within one minute'. Standards make sure **every guest gets the same good service every time**, whoever is on duty. They are not there to punish workers or to replace training.

blocks.h: Repeat guests and word of mouth

blocks.p: A guest who comes back again and again is a **repeat guest** (or regular). Repeat guests save the villa money and often recommend it. Today most guests read **online reviews** before they book, so every guest's stay matters, and your service can be seen by thousands of people.

ul: Villas ask guests for **feedback** (comment cards, a short talk at check-out, online reviews) to learn what is going well and what to improve.
Thank the guest for the feedback, whether it is praise or criticism.
Pass written comments to your supervisor and use them to improve your own work. It is not used to decide which staff to dismiss or to collect addresses for adverts.

head: Part
What it is
Example
rows: Words (verbal)
What you say
'Good afternoon, Mr. Grant, welcome to the villa.'
Tone
How you say it: pace, volume, warmth
Calm, friendly and clear, not rushed or loud
Body language (non-verbal)
Facial expression, posture, eye contact, gestures, distance
A smile, eye contact, an open stance with hands out of pockets

blocks.p: When words and body language disagree, guests believe the body language. 'Welcome' said with folded arms and eyes on a phone does not sound welcome.

blocks.h: Body language that helps and harms

head: Helps
Harms
rows: Facing the guest, open posture, smile
Arms folded, looking at a phone
Eye contact, nodding while listening
Leaning on a wall with hands in pockets
Walking towards an arriving guest
Turning half away to finish talking to a colleague
Standing when you speak to a guest
Waving across the garden and going on with your work

blocks.p: **Active listening** means giving the speaker your full attention, showing that you are listening, and checking that you understood. It is not listening while thinking about your own reply, and it is not talking quickly so the other person cannot speak.

flow: Stop what you are doing and face the guest
Listen without interrupting
Nod and use short encouraging words
Ask a question if you are not sure
Repeat back what you heard
Act

head: Kind
What it does
Example
rows: Closed question
Gets a short answer (yes, no, a number)
'Is the room all right?'  'Shall I bring water?'
Open question
Gets the guest to tell you more; starts with what, how, which, tell me
'What would you like to do tomorrow?'  'How was your journey?'

blocks.p: To find out a guest's needs, use **open questions** and listen to the answers. Do not guess from clothes or wait for a complaint.

ul: Use **clear, simple English** with visitors and avoid heavy local slang. This is not because slang is rude or against the law. It is so the visitor fully understands you.
If you do not understand a guest, ask politely once more, then **repeat back** what you heard. Never nod and guess, never say their accent is too hard, never walk away.
With a guest who speaks very little English, speak **slowly** with simple words, use gestures and a written note, and use a translation app if you have one. Do not shout and do not speak faster.
Learn a few words of the guests' languages (Spanish, French, German) for greeting and thanks.

blocks.p: Thank the guest, ask whether there is anything else you can do, and say how to contact you. Do not walk off as soon as you finish speaking.

blocks.note: Keep your guest conversations friendly but professional. Do not discuss your own problems, other guests' private matters or politics with guests.
blocks.label: Tip

flow: Answer quickly, within the standard (often by the third ring)
Greet the caller, say the villa's name and your own name
Listen and write notes
Help, or find out and call back
Repeat important details
Thank the caller and let them hang up first

ul: Speak clearly and smile: the caller can hear it in your voice.
Say 'May I put you on hold?' and wait for the answer. Never put the phone down on the desk with 'Hold on'.
If you must call someone, say who you are transferring the call to.
Use a clear, polite voice even if you are busy.

blocks.p: A good message lets the person act without calling you to ask what it was about. Write it on a message pad or in the log book, and pass it on **quickly**.

head: Include
Example
rows: Who the message is for
Mrs. Campbell (villa manager)
Caller's name and number (repeat it back)
Mr. Henry Brown, 876 555 0123
The message
Asks for a pick-up at the airport on Friday
Date and time of the call
Tuesday 2 June, 10:15 a.m.
Your name and any action
Taken by Kerry-Ann; I told him the manager would call back by noon

blocks.note: Do not write your opinion of the caller's voice or manner in the message.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.note: When you give out a guest's details, remember privacy. Do not give out a guest's room, phone number or movements to a caller. Offer to take a message instead.
blocks.label: Safety

sections.title: Finding out and meeting guest needs

ul: Read the booking notes: names, number of adults and children, arrival time, special requests, allergies and occasions.
Prepare what is needed: cots, high chairs, extra towels, a welcome drink, a ground-floor room.
Brief the team, so everyone knows.

head: Guest
What to do
What not to do
rows: Family with young children
Offer a clean, safe cot or high chair, child-friendly meals at suitable times
Show the pool gate and steps, and remind parents that children must be watched near water
Ask what the children like to eat
Place hot dishes or sharp knives near a child; seat the family away from everyone else
Older guest who finds steps hard
Offer help and ask the manager about a ground-floor room
Walk beside the guest and offer an arm only if wanted
Tell the guest to be quicker; pick the guest up without asking; leave a guest struggling who has not said anything
Guest who uses a wheelchair
Ask 'How can I help?' and listen to the answer
Speak to the guest, not only to the companion
Check ramps, door widths, bathroom access
Push the chair without asking; speak loudly and slowly as if the guest cannot hear
Guest with difficulty hearing
Face the guest so lips can be seen, speak clearly at normal volume
Reduce background noise, write things down, use gestures
Shout; turn away when speaking; cover your mouth
Guest who speaks little English
Speak slowly, short sentences, simple words, gestures
Point to menus or photographs; use a translation app
Shout; speak faster; avoid the guest
Guest with a food allergy
Ask exactly what the guest cannot eat
Check with the cook and tell the guest what you find out
Tell the whole team and write it in the log book
Guess that a dish is safe; say 'a little will not hurt'

head: Word
What it usually means
rows: Vegetarian
No meat, poultry or fish (may include eggs and dairy)
Vegan
No animal products at all, including eggs, dairy and honey
Ital
A way of eating followed by many Rastafarians: natural, mostly plant foods with little or no salt
Gluten-free
No wheat, barley or rye
Halal / kosher
Prepared by the religious rules of Muslim / Jewish guests; ask what the guest needs
Allergy
A reaction that can be dangerous, such as to nuts, shellfish, eggs or milk. Always take seriously

ul: Treat every guest with equal respect, whatever the country, religion or language.
Learn about customs and ask politely: how to address a guest, what foods to avoid, how to greet.
Never give your best service to guests from one country only.

Give **honest recommendations**. When a family asks for a place to eat in Negril, suggest ideas that suit their taste and budget, not only your cousin's restaurant. If you do not know the answer, say 'I will find out' and **come back** with it. Never make up an answer.

blocks.note: Guests who need extra help are sometimes called guests with special needs. Always ask the guest what help is wanted instead of assuming.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: A guest who complains is giving you a chance to put things right. A guest who is unhappy and says nothing may leave and write a bad review. Do not take a complaint personally.

flow: Listen: let the guest finish without interrupting, stay calm
Apologise: 'I'm sorry this happened'
Solve: do what you can, or call your supervisor
Thank: for telling you, and follow up later

head: Say
Do not say
rows: 'I am sorry this happened. Let me sort it out for you.'
'It's not my fault.'
'Let me find the manager for you right now.'
'Other guests never complained about this.'
'Thank you for telling me.'
'You should have told us yesterday.'

ul: Put the problem right as quickly as you can. This is called **service recovery**.

If it is beyond your power (a refund, a room change, a repair you cannot do), **tell your supervisor quickly and keep the guest informed**. Do not promise a refund you cannot give, and do not tell the guest nothing can be done.
**Write it down** on a complaint form or in the log book: date, time, guest, the problem and the action taken.
**Check back** later that the guest is happy. Do not avoid the guest afterwards.
Never charge the guest for the repair, ask the guest not to complain again, or blame colleagues or the maintenance team.

flow: Stay calm, speak quietly and slowly
Listen and show empathy ('I can see this is upsetting')
Do not argue, swear or raise your voice
Offer to fix the problem
Call the supervisor if it goes on or you feel unsafe

ul: **Empathy** means understanding and sharing how another person feels.
You may move to a safe place and call your supervisor if a guest becomes threatening.
Never tell other guests about the rude guest. Record what happened privately.

blocks.note: Never argue with a guest or another worker in front of guests. It upsets people and harms the villa's good name. If you need to discuss a problem, go to a private place.
blocks.label: Remember

flow: Make the area safe, and do not move a person who may be badly hurt
Call for trained help at once (the first aider, 110 for ambulance)
Stay with the guest and keep them calm
Tell the supervisor
Write an accident report

ul: Do not ask the guest to sign a form before you help. Do not finish another task first. Do not lift the guest if they may have a back or neck injury.
Emergency numbers in Jamaica: 119 police, 110 fire and ambulance.

blocks.p: In a villa the cook, the housekeeper, the gardener, the pool attendant, the driver and the manager all serve the same guests. When the team works well, work is done well and guests receive better service. When it does not, the guest feels it first.

blocks.h: What a good team member does

ul: Arrives on time and is ready to work.
Shares work fairly. Takes a turn at the unpleasant tasks.
**Helps** a busy colleague when your own tasks are done (with tasks you are trained to do). Do not take a long break or go home early without telling the supervisor.
Welcomes and shows new workers. If a new colleague does not know where the cleaning supplies are, show him where they are and explain the system. Do not laugh at him.
Passes information clearly. A guest's special request is told directly to the colleague and written down as well.
Never talks about a colleague behind their back, never takes credit for someone else's work, never leaves dirty dishes for others.

blocks.h: Lifting and carrying as a team

blocks.p: Ask a colleague to help with a heavy box. Lift together with straight backs and bent knees. Do not lift alone to avoid looking weak, ask a guest to help, or leave it in a doorway.

head: Routine
What it is for
rows: Roster
A written timetable of who works which shift and which duties
Team briefing (start of shift)
Share the day's plans, arrivals, special guest needs and tasks
Duty plan
Who does what, and when, for a particular job such as preparing for an arrival
Log book
A shared book in which staff write notes and requests for the next shift
Handover (end of shift)
Pass on to the next shift what is done and what is still to do

flow: Walk the area and check what is done
Write the handover sheet or log book entry
Give it face to face and talk it through
The next person reads it back and asks questions
Sign and date

blocks.p: A handover note should include **guest requests, unfinished jobs and any problems** (such as a leaking tap, a broken lamp or a guest complaint still open). It should not include gossip, complaints about colleagues you do not like, or the guests' tips. It is needed at every shift change, whether or not the manager is at the villa.
People disagree. The aim is to settle it calmly and fairly, **out of sight and hearing of guests**.

flow: Stay calm and talk privately
Each person says what the problem is, without blaming
Check the facts (the roster, the duty plan)
Agree what is fair and write it down if helpful
Ask the supervisor if you cannot agree

head: Do
Do not
rows: Talk calmly and check the roster
Shout until one gives in
Ask the supervisor to help
Leave the job undone until the manager notices
Keep it private
Ask guests to vote or take sides

sections.title: Working with your supervisor, and presenting yourself

ul: If you do not fully understand an instruction, **ask questions until you are sure, before you start**. Do not guess, ask a guest, or do a different job and say nothing.
Repeat the instruction back in your own words and note the time it is needed.
When your supervisor says your work is not to standard, **listen**, ask how to improve and practise the right way. Do not argue, complain to guests or stop doing the job.
Feedback helps you improve, and good workers use it. It is not a personal attack.

blocks.p: A friendly, positive attitude makes guests feel welcome and valued and makes teamwork easier. It does not mean you can ignore rules, and it is not only for days when guests tip. If you are having a bad day at home, keep your problems private and stay professional. Do not tell guests your problems, avoid guests, or be short with them.

head: Area
Standard
rows: Uniform
Clean, pressed, name badge in place
Hair and hands
Neat hair (tied back if working with food), short clean nails, hands washed often
Fragrance and jewellery
Light scent only; no jingling bracelets
Behaviour
Polite, on time, no phones when working with guests

ul: Wash hands before handling glasses and food.
Keep floors dry; put out a wet floor sign after mopping.
Read the label and wear gloves when using cleaning chemicals; never mix products.
Report hazards to your supervisor.

blocks.note: In Jamaican hospitality, guests often notice friendliness before anything else. Greet with a warm 'Good morning', 'Good afternoon' or 'Good evening'. It is a good habit that tourists remember.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: Tick each statement when you can do it without looking at your notes.

ul: I can explain what good customer service is and give examples of meeting and exceeding expectations.
I can greet a guest with words, tone and body language that match.
I can listen actively and use open questions to find out needs.
I can speak clear, simple English and cope with a guest who speaks little English.
I can answer the villa phone and take a complete message.
I can meet the needs of families, older guests, guests with a disability and guests with a dietary need or allergy.
I can handle a complaint using Listen, Apologise, Solve, Thank, and follow up.
I can stay calm and safe with a rude guest and know when to call my supervisor.
I can respond when a guest is hurt.
I can take part in a briefing, share work, help colleagues and write a handover note.
I can solve a conflict calmly and privately.
I can take instructions and feedback from my supervisor and present myself professionally.

terms: Meeting, and going beyond, what a guest needs and expects
Giving better service than the guest expected
A guest who stays again and again
A written promise about how a task is done
Messages sent without words, such as expression and posture
Full attention, showing you listen and checking you understood
A question that invites a longer answer
Understanding and sharing how another person feels
Putting things right after something has gone wrong
A written record of a complaint and what was done
Shared book of notes for the next shift
A short meeting to share plans and needs
Passing on information at the end of a shift
The person who leads the team on a shift and checks its work
A plant-based way of eating followed by many Rastafarians

c1.title: The Thompsons arrive at a villa in Runaway Bay
c1.text: The Thompson family arrives at a villa in Runaway Bay at 3:00 p.m. after a long flight from Toronto: two parents and twin girls aged five. The booking notes say they asked for two cots and that one girl is allergic to peanuts. Housekeeper Shanice is in the garden when their car pulls up, and she is tired because she has been working since 6:00 a.m. Behind her, her supervisor Mr. Williams is on the phone.

c2.title: A phone call about an airport pick-up
c2.text: At the same villa, the phone rings. Trainee Kemoy answers it. The caller is Mr. Alan Peters, who is booking for next month. He wants to know whether the villa can arrange a pick-up from Montego Bay airport, and he speaks quickly with a strong accent. The villa manager, Mrs. Harris, is out until noon. Kemoy writes on the back of his hand because he cannot find the message pad.

c3.title: A complaint about a damp-smelling room
c3.text: Mrs. Doreen Clarke, a guest at a guest house in Port Royal, comes to the desk at 8:30 a.m. She says that her bed linen smells damp and that she hardly slept. She is upset and speaks loudly while other guests are having breakfast nearby. Front desk worker Nathan did not make the bed and the housekeeper, Pauline, is off today. The manager is not due until 10:00 a.m.

c4.title: A missed handover note
c4.text: Garth works the evening shift and Tricia the morning shift. Last night, Garth was asked by a guest, Mr. Barnes, for an early breakfast at 6:00 a.m. because of a tour. Garth meant to write it in the log book but left in a hurry. The next morning, Tricia is not told, and Mr. Barnes comes to the dining area at 6:00 and finds nothing ready. He is annoyed, and Tricia and the cook, Winston, begin blaming each other loudly in the kitchen doorway.

c5.title: Guests who need extra help in Falmouth
c5.text: A villa near Falmouth has booked a Spanish-speaking couple, Mr. and Mrs. Garcia, who speak very little English, and Mr. Ainsworth, an older guest with a hearing difficulty who comes with his daughter. The villa also has a broken ramp rail on its front steps.

c6.title: Feedback for a new worker
c6.text: Natalie is new at a villa in Treasure Beach. Her supervisor, Mrs. Pryce, checks the rooms and tells her that the corners of her beds are not tight enough and the towels are not folded to the villa's standard. Natalie feels embarrassed. She thinks of telling the guests that Mrs. Pryce is too strict.

questions.q: What should Shanice do when the Thompsons' car pulls up?
o: Finish her task, then greet them when they come in
Stop her work, walk to the car, smile and greet them
Wave from the garden and keep working
Wait for Mr. Williams to finish his call
questions.why: The first minute sets the tone, so Shanice should stop, approach with a smile and greet them warmly. Waving from a distance or waiting does not make guests feel welcome.

questions.q: Shanice greets the whole family, including the girls. What helps her to find out what they need?
o: Ask closed questions only, so the answers are short
Guess from the children's age what they need
Wait for the parents to ask for whatever they want
Ask open questions and listen to the answers
questions.why: Open questions invite guests to tell you more, and listening to the answers shows what they need. Guessing or waiting may miss something important.

questions.q: The notes say one girl is allergic to peanuts. What is the best action?
o: Tell the cook and the team, and write it in the log book
Tell only the cook, as no one else prepares meals
Trust the parents to check every dish themselves
Keep the information private so the family is not embarrassed
questions.why: An allergy can be dangerous, so the whole team must know and it must be written down so every shift follows it. Treating it as private could put the child at risk.

questions.q: How should Kemoy answer the phone?
o: Say 'Yes?' and wait for the caller to speak
Say 'Hold on' and put the phone down while he looks for a pen
Greet the caller, say the villa's name and then his own name
Ask the caller to ring back at noon
questions.why: A standard greeting gives the caller confidence that he has reached the right place and who is helping. A bare 'Yes?' or 'Hold on' sounds careless.

questions.q: Mr. Peters speaks quickly and Kemoy cannot follow. What should he do?
o: Tell Mr. Peters politely that his accent is too hard to follow
Agree with what he says and guess what the caller probably wants
Ask politely for the request again, then repeat back what he heard
Say that the manager will call back and then hang up quickly
questions.why: Asking again and repeating back is the way to be sure you understood, without blaming the caller. Guessing can lead to the wrong booking.

questions.q: What should Kemoy's message for Mrs. Harris include?
o: The caller's name and number, the request, the date and time, his name
Only the caller's first name, so that she can phone him back
His opinion of the caller's manner and the sound of his voice
A short note that someone called about a pick-up from the airport
questions.why: A message must let the manager act without asking Kemoy what it meant. Opinions and vague notes are not enough.

questions.q: Mrs. Clarke is upset and speaks loudly. What should Nathan do first?
o: Tell her quietly that it is not his job
Explain that housekeeping is off today
Ask her to lower her voice before he will talk
Listen without interrupting, stay calm and apologise
questions.why: Listening and apologising calms an upset guest and shows you take the problem seriously. Excuses or ordering her to be quiet make it worse.

questions.q: Nathan cannot change the linen himself because he is not trained or has no key. What is the best step?
o: Promise Mrs. Clarke a full refund so that she will calm down at once
Tell his supervisor or the manager quickly and keep the guest informed
Tell her that nothing can be done about the linen until tomorrow
Ask her to write a letter of complaint to the owner of the guest house
questions.why: When a problem is beyond your power, escalate it quickly and keep the guest informed. Do not promise what you cannot give or leave her without help.

questions.q: After the linen is changed, what should Nathan do?
o: Keep away from her for the rest of her stay to avoid more trouble
Check later that Mrs. Clarke is happy and record the complaint
Ask her not to mention the problem in any review she writes
Add the cost of washing the linen to her bill at check-out
questions.why: Following up shows you care, and recording the complaint lets the villa find the cause. Avoiding the guest or charging her would harm the relationship.

questions.q: Why did the handover fail?
o: The cook did not like Tricia and would not help her with the early breakfast
Mr. Barnes did not make his request clear enough when he asked for it
The request was not written down or passed on at the end of the shift
The roster for the week was printed late and had the wrong names on it
questions.why: A guest's request must go in the log book or on the handover sheet and be passed on. Without it, the next shift cannot know.

questions.q: What should Tricia and Winston do about the argument?
o: Stop, apologise to Mr. Barnes and talk it over later in private
Carry on arguing until they find out which of them is to blame
Ask Mr. Barnes to decide which of the two workers is at fault
Walk away from the dining area and leave Mr. Barnes without help
questions.why: Arguing in front of a guest harms the villa's name. The first need is to look after Mr. Barnes; the discussion should be private and about fixing the system.

questions.q: What is the best immediate help for Mr. Barnes?
o: Tell him politely that breakfast starts at 7:00 a.m. as it does every day
Offer him a discount on a future stay and leave the breakfast to the cook
Explain to him that the evening worker forgot to write down the request
Apologise, offer a drink and a simple breakfast, and tell the supervisor
questions.why: Putting things right quickly is service recovery. Explaining the fault to the guest or offering something later does not solve his problem.

questions.q: Which change would best prevent this problem in the future?
o: Ask guests to tell each worker about their requests themselves
Give workers longer breaks so that they are not in a hurry to leave
Let each worker decide for themselves what to pass on to the next shift
Write every guest request in the log book and read it out at the briefing
questions.why: A shared written system and a briefing make sure everyone sees the same information. It does not depend on one person's memory.

questions.q: What is the best way to help Mr. and Mrs. Garcia?
o: Speak louder and faster so that they can hear every word you say
Speak slowly with simple words and gestures, and use a translation app
Ask another guest who knows a little Spanish to speak for them all day
Wait for them to learn enough English to ask you for what they want
questions.why: Slow, simple speech, gestures and a translation tool help understanding. Shouting or speeding up does not.

questions.q: How should staff talk with Mr. Ainsworth, who has a hearing difficulty?
o: Shout from across the room so that he can hear every word
Talk only to his daughter, who can hear without any difficulty
Face him, speak clearly at normal volume, and write things down
Speak very quickly so that he has no time to ask you to repeat
questions.why: Facing him lets him see your lips and expressions. Shouting is uncomfortable, and speaking to his daughter excludes him.

questions.q: Mr. Ainsworth finds the front steps hard. What should the villa do?
o: Offer help and ask whether a ground-floor room is possible
Tell him to take the steps slowly and carefully by himself
Carry him up the steps at once without asking his permission
Leave him alone with the steps unless he makes a complaint
questions.why: Offer help, listen to what he wants and look for a room with easier access. Do not assume or force help on him.

questions.q: How should Natalie respond to Mrs. Pryce's feedback?
o: Listen, ask how to improve, and practise the right way
Explain to Mrs. Pryce that her own way of making beds is faster
Tell the guests that the supervisor is too strict with new workers
Ask another worker to make the beds so she is not checked again
questions.why: Feedback is a chance to improve, and a good worker uses it. Complaining to guests harms the villa and the team.

questions.q: What is the best way for Natalie to improve her bed-making?
o: Copy the way she makes beds at home since that is how she learned
Do the beds faster so that there is less time for anyone to check
Pull the corners tight on one bed and leave the others as they are
Ask Mrs. Pryce to show the villa's method, then practise it
questions.why: Asking to be shown the villa's own standard and practising it is how skills improve. Doing it your own way or rushing does not meet the standard.

questions.q: A guest tells you she is vegan. Which food is suitable for her?
o: A dish with no meat but cooked with cheese
A dish with no meat, fish, eggs, dairy or honey
A dish with no meat or fish but topped with a fried egg
A dish with no red meat but with chicken stock
questions.why: Vegan means no animal products at all. Vegetarian guests may eat eggs or dairy, but vegans do not.

questions.q: Mrs. Clarke says she will post a bad review. What is the best reply?
o: Ask her to wait until the manager arrives and say nothing more
Tell her that no other guest has ever complained about the bed
Thank her for telling you, say you will put it right, and follow up
Say that reviews are written by guests who did not read the rules
questions.why: Thanking a guest for the complaint, promising action and following up is the best way to keep the guest. Excuses or arguing about the review make her less likely to change her mind.
